chapter: The craft of the ad lib player
title: Booking agents, record companies and the rush to record tenor players
summary: Hall describes the rat race for work, record companies floundering and Sonny Rollins being rushed.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: Well, what about the -- the end of the business that we were talking about off mike earlier, you know, the promises, promises idea and all the things you run into with people, you know, the promoters and the bookers and the record company people and the club owners and things like this that you ought to touch on. Or are we getting ahead of ourselves?
No, it's all part of it, I guess.
Because I know you have some things that you wanted to get across.

Our first problem came from the booking agents and the lack of work and, hence, the rat race that Nick named it of trying to get a job. You (inaudible) trying to get a job. I don't think I'd be able to go through that. And then it became a sort of militarized situation, and he couldn't go over anyone's head, and you had your yard dogs and your generals and all in between. (Laughter.) And that depended upon your employment.

Then the record companies weren't sure of what they wanted to record, and they were floundering and recording a lot of musicians that are great today, but they shouldn't have been recorded then, because they were still in their
In what period are you referring now?

'40, late '40s, '50s. All a guy had to do was have a tenor saxophone during that period, and he recorded. And it wasn't necessarily professional up to the point of Coleman Hawkins or Lester Young. I knew Sonny Rollins when he was a baby. He was put out too fast, and he suffered for it for a length of time, his loneliness and of trying to get himself together, because he was pushed. Then, well, there's mostly for (inaudible) tenor saxophone players, anyhow. Tenors prevailed over altos, trumpet players, and whatnot that kind of thing, bass players. It was, well, the bass players, after Jimmy Blanton, they changed the whole schmear around. There have been some terrific guys, but he created it at the time that he did. Maybe that's why he died so early. He didn't have any more to contribute after that.
